questiontext.text: In the testability sense, what does controllability measure?

answer.text: How well a test can DRIVE the system into the states/inputs it needs to exercise

feedback.text: Correct — controllability is the "drive it there" half of testability.

answer.text: How well a test can SEE the effects it needs to check

feedback.text: That is observability, the other half of testability.

answer.text: How many states the model has

feedback.text: A raw state count is not controllability; controllability is about reachability by inputs.

answer.text: How many transitions are covered by a test suite

feedback.text: That is transition coverage, a different idea from controllability.

generalfeedback.text: Controllability asks whether a test can drive the software into the states and inputs it must exercise. Hidden state, unreachable branches, and hard-coded dependencies all reduce it.

questiontext.text: In the testability sense, what does observability measure?

answer.text: How well a test can DRIVE the system into a chosen state

feedback.text: That is controllability, not observability.

answer.text: How well a test can SEE the effects/outputs it needs to check

feedback.text: Correct — observability is the "can I see it" half of testability.

answer.text: How many inputs the system accepts

feedback.text: The number of inputs is not observability; observability is about distinguishable outputs.

answer.text: How fast the test suite runs

feedback.text: Speed is unrelated to observability.

generalfeedback.text: Observability asks whether a test can see the effects it needs to check. Side effects, swallowed errors, and missing/return outputs that collide with other states all reduce it.

questiontext.text: Testability is classically defined as controllability + observability — a system is testable to the degree a test can both drive it into the needed states and observe the resulting effects.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — both halves are required; either one alone is not enough.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Testability is exactly controllability together with observability.

generalfeedback.text: The classical definition (control-theory roots; Freedman; Binder) is testability = controllability + observability. You must be able to drive the SUT to the situation you want AND see the effect to check it.

questiontext.text: In the turnstile model, what is a reachable state?

answer.text: A state that some sequence of test inputs, starting from the start state, can drive the SUT into

feedback.text: Correct — reachability here means "an input sequence from the start gets you there".

answer.text: A state whose output value is unique

feedback.text: That describes an observable state, not a reachable one.

answer.text: Only the start state

feedback.text: The start state is reachable, but so is any state an input sequence can enter.

answer.text: Any state that has a self-loop

feedback.text: Self-loops are unrelated to whether a state can be reached from the start.

generalfeedback.text: reachableStates(sut) does a BFS from the start over the input-driven transitions. A state is reachable when some input sequence from the start arrives there.

questiontext.text: What does it mean that a state is unreachable by the test in this model?

answer.text: The state has no observable output

feedback.text: Reachability is about input-driven transitions, not about outputs.

answer.text: The state is the start state

feedback.text: The start state is always reachable; unreachable is the opposite.

answer.text: No sequence of test inputs from the start can drive the SUT into it

feedback.text: Correct — no input path leads there, so a test cannot set it up.

answer.text: The state has more than one outgoing transition

feedback.text: Having outgoing transitions does not make a state unreachable.

generalfeedback.text: An unreachable state has no input-driven path into it from the start, so a test cannot drive the SUT there. In the turnstile, JAMMED and MAINT are unreachable by the test's inputs — the controllability gap.

questiontext.text: In this model, what is an observable output?

answer.text: An internal state variable the test cannot read

feedback.text: The point of an output is that it CAN be seen from outside; a hidden variable is the opposite.

answer.text: A value a test can see from outside the SUT (such as 'red', 'green', or 'beep')

feedback.text: Correct — outputs are the externally visible projection a test checks.

answer.text: The input event that triggers a transition

feedback.text: That is an input (coin/push/reset), not an output.

answer.text: A transition edge in the state graph

feedback.text: An edge is a transition; an output is the visible value of a state.

generalfeedback.text: Each state maps to an observable output in sut.outputs — the value a test can see from outside (e.g. LOCKED→'red', PASSED→'beep'). Observability is measured over these outputs.

answer.text: red

feedback.text: red is shared by LOCKED and MAINT, so it is not unique.

questiontext.text: In this engine, when is a state's fault considered observable?

answer.text: When the state's output value is unique — no other state shares it

feedback.text: Correct — a unique output lets an observer distinguish that state, so a fault landing there is visible.

answer.text: When the state is reachable from the start

feedback.text: Reachability is controllability; observability is about distinguishable outputs.

answer.text: When the state is the start state

feedback.text: Being the start has nothing to do with whether a fault there is observable.

answer.text: When the state has a self-loop

feedback.text: Self-loops do not determine observability.

generalfeedback.text: observableStates(sut) keeps a state only when its output value is unique across all states. A shared output means an observer cannot tell those states apart, so a fault there is invisible.

feedback.text: Two states (JAMMED, MAINT) are unreachable, so it is not 5/5.

questiontext.text: Starting from LOCKED and using only the inputs coin/push/reset, which set of states can the test reach?

answer.text: {LOCKED, UNLOCKED, PASSED}

feedback.text: Correct — coin reaches UNLOCKED, push reaches PASSED, reset returns to LOCKED; JAMMED and MAINT are never entered.

answer.text: {LOCKED, UNLOCKED, PASSED, JAMMED, MAINT}

feedback.text: JAMMED and MAINT have no input-driven edge into them, so they are not reachable.

answer.text: {LOCKED, UNLOCKED}

feedback.text: PASSED is also reachable via coin then push.

answer.text: {LOCKED, UNLOCKED, PASSED, JAMMED}

feedback.text: JAMMED is entered only by a fault, not by any input, so it is not reachable.

generalfeedback.text: BFS from LOCKED over the input edges reaches UNLOCKED (coin) and PASSED (coin, push), and reset only returns to LOCKED. No edge leads into JAMMED or MAINT, so the reachable set is exactly {LOCKED, UNLOCKED, PASSED}.

questiontext.text: Why can the test not drive the turnstile into JAMMED?

answer.text: No input-driven transition leads INTO JAMMED — it is entered only by a fault, not by any test input

feedback.text: Correct — with no incoming input edge, no input sequence can arrive at JAMMED.

answer.text: Because JAMMED has no outgoing transitions

feedback.text: JAMMED does have an outgoing edge (reset→LOCKED); the problem is that nothing leads in.

answer.text: Because JAMMED shares its output with UNLOCKED

feedback.text: That shared output is the observability gap, not the reason JAMMED is unreachable.

answer.text: Because JAMMED is the start state

feedback.text: LOCKED is the start; JAMMED is not.

generalfeedback.text: Reachability depends on edges INTO a state. The only edge touching JAMMED is JAMMED--reset-->LOCKED (outgoing). Since no input drives anything into JAMMED, a fault is the only way in — the controllability gap.

questiontext.text: Why can the test not drive the turnstile into MAINT?

answer.text: Because MAINT shares the output 'red' with LOCKED

feedback.text: The shared output is an observability issue; it does not explain unreachability.

answer.text: No transition leads into MAINT — it is entered only by a maintenance key, which is not one of the test's inputs

feedback.text: Correct — MAINT has no incoming input edge, so no input sequence reaches it.

answer.text: Because MAINT has a self-loop that traps the machine

feedback.text: MAINT has no edges at all in the model; there is no self-loop involved.

answer.text: Because reset always leads away from MAINT

feedback.text: There is no reset edge from MAINT; the point is nothing leads INTO it.

generalfeedback.text: MAINT is entered only by a maintenance key, which is deliberately NOT among inputs = [coin, push, reset]. With no input edge into MAINT, it is unreachable by the test — part of the controllability gap.

questiontext.text: What input sequence does driveTo(TURNSTILE_SUT, 'PASSED') return (the shortest path from the start)?

feedback.text: Correct — LOCKED--coin-->UNLOCKED--push-->PASSED.

feedback.text: push alone from LOCKED loops back to LOCKED and never reaches PASSED.

answer.text: coin

name.text: Why a fault in JAMMED is invisible

questiontext.text: In the base model, why would a fault that lands in JAMMED be invisible to a test watching the output?

answer.text: Because JAMMED emits 'beep', the same as PASSED

feedback.text: JAMMED emits 'green', not 'beep'; beep is unique to PASSED.

answer.text: Because JAMMED's output 'green' is shared with UNLOCKED, so the observer cannot tell them apart

feedback.text: Correct — colliding outputs make the two states indistinguishable, hiding the fault.

answer.text: Because JAMMED is the start state

feedback.text: LOCKED is the start; JAMMED is not, and that is unrelated to visibility.

answer.text: Because JAMMED has no output at all

feedback.text: JAMMED does have an output ('green'); the issue is that it collides with UNLOCKED.

generalfeedback.text: JAMMED→'green' and UNLOCKED→'green'. When a fault drops the SUT into JAMMED, the output still reads 'green', identical to a normal UNLOCKED, so the observer cannot detect the jam — the observability gap.

questiontext.text: Which two states share the output value 'red'?

answer.text: LOCKED and MAINT

feedback.text: Correct — both map to 'red', so neither is observable in the base model.

answer.text: UNLOCKED and JAMMED

feedback.text: Those two share 'green', not 'red'.

feedback.text: LOCKED is 'red' but UNLOCKED is 'green'; they do not share.

answer.text: PASSED and MAINT

feedback.text: PASSED is 'beep' and MAINT is 'red'; they do not share.

generalfeedback.text: outputs: LOCKED→'red', MAINT→'red'. Because 'red' is shared, neither LOCKED nor MAINT is observable.

questiontext.text: Which two states share the output value 'green'?

answer.text: LOCKED and MAINT

feedback.text: Those two share 'red', not 'green'.

answer.text: PASSED and JAMMED

feedback.text: PASSED is 'beep'; only JAMMED (with UNLOCKED) is 'green'.

answer.text: UNLOCKED and JAMMED

feedback.text: Correct — both map to 'green', which is exactly why a jam looks like a normal unlock.

answer.text: LOCKED and UNLOCKED

feedback.text: LOCKED is 'red', UNLOCKED is 'green'; they do not share.

generalfeedback.text: outputs: UNLOCKED→'green', JAMMED→'green'. The collision on 'green' is the observability gap that hides a jam.

questiontext.text: What does adding a probe (withProbe) do in this explorer?

answer.text: It gives a state a distinct output so a previously-shared output becomes unique, raising observability — returning a new SUT without mutating the original

feedback.text: Correct — withProbe returns a new outputs map; it is the "observability is a design choice" lever.

answer.text: It adds a new input transition so an unreachable state becomes reachable

feedback.text: That would change controllability; a probe only changes outputs.

answer.text: It deletes an unreachable state from the model

feedback.text: A probe adds a distinguishing output; it removes nothing.

answer.text: It changes which state is the start state

feedback.text: The start state is unchanged; a probe only affects outputs.

generalfeedback.text: withProbe(sut, state, distinctOutput) returns { ...sut, outputs: { ...sut.outputs, [state]: distinctOutput } } — a NEW SUT whose target state now emits a distinct value, so its output stops colliding and it becomes observable.

questiontext.text: After a probe gives JAMMED its own distinct output, which states become observable that were not before?

answer.text: Only JAMMED

feedback.text: UNLOCKED also becomes unique, because 'green' no longer collides once JAMMED has a distinct output.

answer.text: UNLOCKED and JAMMED both become unique

feedback.text: Correct — the probe un-collides 'green', so UNLOCKED and JAMMED are each now the sole owner of their output.

answer.text: LOCKED and MAINT

feedback.text: Those still share 'red'; the JAMMED probe does not touch them.

answer.text: All five states

feedback.text: LOCKED and MAINT still collide on 'red', so not all five are observable.

generalfeedback.text: Before: UNLOCKED and JAMMED both 'green' (neither observable). Probing JAMMED to a distinct value leaves UNLOCKED as the only 'green' and JAMMED as the only holder of the new value, so BOTH become observable — observability rises from 1/5 to 3/5 (PASSED, UNLOCKED, JAMMED).

feedback.text: Finding a driving path is controllability.

questiontext.text: Suppose a maintenance-key input were added that drives the SUT into MAINT (which has no outgoing edges). What would the controllability ratio become?

feedback.text: JAMMED would still be unreachable, so it cannot be 5/5.
That is the current value; adding a reachable MAINT raises it.
Correct — MAINT joins the reachable set {LOCKED, UNLOCKED, PASSED}, giving 4 of 5; JAMMED is still unreachable.
Adding a reachable state increases, not decreases, controllability.

name.text: Why JAMMED's outgoing edge does not help

questiontext.text: JAMMED has the edge JAMMED--reset-->LOCKED. Why does that edge still not let the test reach JAMMED?

answer.text: Reachability needs an edge INTO JAMMED; an outgoing edge lets you leave JAMMED but never arrive there

feedback.text: Correct — you can only take JAMMED--reset-->LOCKED if you are already in JAMMED, which the test cannot achieve.

answer.text: Because reset is not one of the inputs

feedback.text: reset IS an input; the issue is direction — no edge leads into JAMMED.

answer.text: Because JAMMED shares 'green' with UNLOCKED

feedback.text: That is the observability gap; it is unrelated to whether JAMMED can be reached.

answer.text: Because the edge comes after PASSED in the graph

feedback.text: Ordering in the graph does not affect reachability; incoming edges do.

generalfeedback.text: BFS follows edges in their direction. JAMMED--reset-->LOCKED is outgoing, usable only once you are in JAMMED. Since no edge points INTO JAMMED, the test can never get there — the outgoing edge is irrelevant to reachability.

name.text: Why driveTo PASSED needs two steps

questiontext.text: Why is the shortest driving sequence to PASSED exactly two steps (coin, push) and not one?

answer.text: PASSED is entered only by push from UNLOCKED, and UNLOCKED is entered only by coin from LOCKED — so you must do coin then push

feedback.text: Correct — the only path into PASSED forces this two-step chain.

answer.text: Because reset must be sent before push

feedback.text: reset is not on the path to PASSED; coin then push is the route.

answer.text: Because PASSED has a self-loop that must be entered twice

feedback.text: PASSED has no self-loop; the two steps come from the chain LOCKED→UNLOCKED→PASSED.

answer.text: Because JAMMED blocks the direct path

feedback.text: JAMMED is not on any input path; it does not block anything.

generalfeedback.text: The only edge into PASSED is UNLOCKED--push-->PASSED, and the only edge into UNLOCKED is LOCKED--coin-->UNLOCKED. From the start LOCKED that forces the chain coin, push — two steps, the minimum.

questiontext.text: What does a controllability of 3/5 tell you about the turnstile?

answer.text: A test can drive the SUT into 3 of the 5 modeled states; the other 2 (JAMMED, MAINT) are out of its reach

feedback.text: Correct — 3/5 counts input-reachable states over total states.

answer.text: 3 of the 5 outputs are unique

feedback.text: That describes observability, not controllability.

answer.text: 3 of the 5 transitions are exercised by the test suite

feedback.text: Controllability counts reachable states, not exercised transitions.

answer.text: 3 of the 5 inputs are valid

feedback.text: All inputs are valid; the ratio is over states, not inputs.

generalfeedback.text: controllability.ratio = |reachable| / |states| = 3/5. It means the test can set up 3 of the 5 states; JAMMED and MAINT cannot be reached by any input sequence.

questiontext.text: What does an observability of 1/5 tell you about the base turnstile?

answer.text: 3 of the 5 states are reachable

feedback.text: That is controllability, and the number would be 3/5, not 1/5.

answer.text: Only 1 of the 5 states (PASSED) has a distinguishable output; a fault in any of the other 4 can be confused with another state

feedback.text: Correct — 1/5 counts states with a unique output.

answer.text: Exactly 1 of the 5 transitions is covered

feedback.text: Observability counts distinguishable-output states, not covered transitions.

answer.text: 1 of the 5 inputs is never used

feedback.text: The ratio is over states with unique outputs, not over inputs.

generalfeedback.text: observability.ratio = |observable| / |states| = 1/5. Only PASSED→'beep' is unique; LOCKED/MAINT collide on 'red' and UNLOCKED/JAMMED on 'green', so a fault in any of those four is indistinguishable at the output.

questiontext.text: Adding a single probe raises observability from 1/5 to 3/5. What accounts for the jump of two, not one?

answer.text: The probe makes JAMMED reachable by the test's inputs

feedback.text: That would be controllability; a probe changes outputs, not reachability.

answer.text: The probe adds two new states to the model

feedback.text: A probe changes one state's output; it adds no states.

answer.text: Giving JAMMED a distinct output un-collides 'green', so UNLOCKED and JAMMED each become unique, joining PASSED — 3 of 5

feedback.text: Correct — resolving one collision makes BOTH members of the pair unique at once.

answer.text: The probe removes MAINT from the model

feedback.text: Nothing is removed; the gain comes from un-colliding the 'green' pair.

generalfeedback.text: 'green' was shared by UNLOCKED and JAMMED, so neither was observable. Probing JAMMED to a distinct value leaves UNLOCKED as the sole 'green' AND makes JAMMED unique — two states flip to observable at once, so 1/5 becomes 3/5 (PASSED, UNLOCKED, JAMMED).

questiontext.text: Which lever raises observability without changing the state graph — making observability a design choice?

answer.text: Adding a probe / return value that gives a state its own distinct output

feedback.text: Correct — exposing more distinguishing output is a design decision that raises observability.

answer.text: Adding an input transition into an unreachable state

feedback.text: That changes the state graph and raises controllability, not observability.

answer.text: Removing a state from the model

feedback.text: Deleting states does not add distinguishing outputs; it is not the observability lever.

answer.text: Changing which state is the start state

feedback.text: The start state affects reachability, not how distinguishable the outputs are.

generalfeedback.text: Observability is a design choice: by adding probes or return values that give states distinct outputs, a developer makes previously indistinguishable states visible — without altering the transition structure.

questiontext.text: A test needs the turnstile to be in JAMMED to check jam handling, but no sequence of inputs can drive it there. Which testability property is lacking?

answer.text: Controllability

feedback.text: Correct — being unable to drive the SUT into the needed state is a controllability problem.

answer.text: Observability

answer.text: Controllability

feedback.text: The state can be reached; the problem is that the output does not distinguish it.

answer.text: Observability

feedback.text: Correct — indistinguishable outputs are an observability gap.

generalfeedback.text: When two states share an output, a test cannot tell which one it is in. Being unable to see the effect you must check is an observability gap — here 'green' hides a jam behind a normal unlock.

answer.text: No — JAMMED is still unreachable by inputs; the probe raised observability, not controllability

feedback.text: Correct — the two properties are orthogonal; a probe only changes outputs.

feedback.text: Probes affect observability only; they never change reachability.

answer.text: No — because the probe also removed JAMMED from the model

feedback.text: The probe removes nothing; JAMMED remains, just now with a distinct output.

generalfeedback.text: A probe edits outputs (observability). It does not add any input edge into JAMMED, so JAMMED stays unreachable — the test can now SEE a jam if one occurred, but still cannot DRIVE the SUT into one. Controllability and observability are independent.

answer.text: UNLOCKED and JAMMED

feedback.text: The probe just un-collided those two; they are now observable.

answer.text: PASSED and LOCKED

generalfeedback.text: After probing JAMMED: outputs are red→{LOCKED, MAINT}, green→{UNLOCKED}, beep→{PASSED}, plus JAMMED's new value. Observable = {UNLOCKED, PASSED, JAMMED} = 3/5; LOCKED and MAINT still collide on 'red'.

questiontext.text: Starting from the 3/5 state (after the JAMMED probe), you add one more probe giving MAINT a distinct output. What does observability become?

feedback.text: Resolving the 'red' collision makes BOTH LOCKED and MAINT unique at once, so it jumps past 4/5.
That is the value before this second probe; adding it raises observability further.
Adding a distinguishing output raises, not lowers, observability.
Correct — un-colliding 'red' makes LOCKED the sole 'red' and MAINT unique, so all five states are now observable.

generalfeedback.text: Just as with 'green', 'red' was shared by exactly two states. Giving MAINT a distinct output leaves LOCKED as the only 'red' and makes MAINT unique — both flip to observable, so 3/5 becomes 5/5.

questiontext.text: Which single change would raise the controllability of the turnstile?

answer.text: Give JAMMED a distinct output

feedback.text: That raises observability, not controllability.

answer.text: Add an input-driven transition leading INTO JAMMED or MAINT

feedback.text: Correct — a new incoming input edge makes an unreachable state reachable, raising controllability.

answer.text: Add a return value that exposes PASSED

feedback.text: PASSED is already reachable AND observable; adding an output does not change controllability.

answer.text: Rename an output value

feedback.text: Renaming an output cannot change which states are reachable.

generalfeedback.text: Controllability depends on the transition structure. Only adding an input-driven edge INTO an unreachable state (JAMMED or MAINT) can raise it; changing outputs affects observability instead.

questiontext.text: Controllability and observability are independent: raising one (for example by adding a probe) does not necessarily raise the other.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a probe raises observability but leaves reachability (controllability) unchanged, and vice versa.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: They are orthogonal: a probe on JAMMED raises observability yet JAMMED stays unreachable.

generalfeedback.text: The two halves of testability are separate levers. Probes change outputs (observability); new input edges change reachability (controllability). Improving one does not automatically improve the other — the JAMMED probe raises observability while controllability of JAMMED stays zero.

name.text: Shortest steps to drive to PASSED

questiontext.text: How many input steps does the shortest sequence that drives TURNSTILE_SUT from the start to PASSED take? Answer with a single integer.

feedback.text: Correct — driveTo returns [coin, push], a length-2 sequence.

generalfeedback.text: The only route into PASSED is LOCKED--coin-->UNLOCKED--push-->PASSED, so the shortest driving sequence has exactly 2 steps.
